opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. Right now Deep Research usually runs for somewhere between five and thirty minutes, and even in that window it can do what would take a person several hours: searching, reading dozens of sources, reconciling conflicting information, and writing it up. So if you extend that to a full day, you start moving from "answer my question" to "do a real project for me."

The first thing that comes to mind is work that today would take a skilled analyst days or weeks: a comprehensive literature review in a scientific field, a thorough market landscape, or a due diligence report where you need to chase down every primary source and cross-check claims. With more time, the model doesn't just gather more; it can go deeper. It can notice that two sources disagree, go find a third to resolve it, realize its initial framing of the question was wrong, and backtrack. That kind of iterative, self-correcting research is what humans spend most of their time on, and it's where longer horizons really pay off.

Longer term, I think the exciting part is combining that browsing and reasoning with other tools. If the agent can also run code, analyze data, and work with your private documents, not just the public web, then a day-long task could look like: pull the data, run the analysis, check it against the literature, and hand you something close to a finished deliverable. Eventually you'd hope it could contribute to genuinely new knowledge, not just synthesizing what's already out there.

The honest caveat is that running longer only helps if the model stays on track. Small errors compound over long trajectories, so a lot of the work is making it reliable enough that hour eight is still as careful as minute one, and knowing when to check back in with the user instead of charging ahead on a wrong assumption. But if we get that right, a day of agent time could be pretty transformative for knowledge work.

r001.rationale: It says a full-day run could handle work that takes a skilled analyst “days or weeks,” including a comprehensive literature review.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think that's a really fun question, because right now Deep Research runs for something like five to thirty minutes, and even in that window it's already doing things that would take a person several hours. So when I imagine it running for a whole day, the first thing that changes isn't just that it reads more sources, it's that it can actually iterate on its own work.

Right now the model does a lot of searching, reading, synthesizing, but it's mostly a single pass. If you gave it a day, it could draft a report, notice the gaps in its own argument, go back and fill them, run little experiments or write code to check a claim, and then rewrite. That loop, where it critiques itself and revises, is where a lot of the quality in human research comes from, and it's really hard to compress into twenty minutes.

Concretely, I think you'd see it do things like a genuinely thorough literature review for a scientific question, where it doesn't just summarize the top ten papers but actually traces citations, reconciles conflicting results, and comes back with "here's what the field agrees on, here's where the evidence is thin, and here are the experiments nobody has run yet." Or in a business context, a full competitive analysis where it's pulled filings, pricing pages, job postings, and built a model out of them rather than just describing them.

The thing I'd caution is that longer isn't automatically better. A lot of what we had to work on with Deep Research was teaching the model to know when to stop, when a source isn't trustworthy, when it's going down a rabbit hole. If you just let it run for a day without that judgment, you get a very long, very confident document that's not actually more useful. So the real unlock for a day-long task is the model being good at planning and verifying, not just having more time. But we train these models with reinforcement learning on exactly those behaviors, so I'm pretty optimistic that the horizon keeps extending, and a day of autonomous work ends up feeling pretty normal sooner than people expect.

r001.rationale: The response describes day-long research as enabling iteration and thorough literature reviews, but does not say it could complete work that would take a human weeks.

astra-6.text:
If it could work for an entire day, I’d want it to tackle questions where each thing it learns changes what it needs to investigate next. So instead of just producing a longer report, it could form a hypothesis, look for evidence, discover that an assumption was wrong, and go down a different path.

You could imagine giving it a research question you’ve been stuck on, or asking it to really understand a problem your business is facing. It could explore several approaches, check them against one another, and come back with something that helps you decide what to do next. The exciting part is whether that extra time translates into deeper investigation and more reliable conclusions.

r001.rationale: The response describes deeper, iterative research over a full day, but does not suggest it could complete work that would take a human weeks.

sol-6.1.text: I think the exciting thing is that it could take on a question where you don’t even know all the subquestions upfront. It could spend time exploring, find something surprising, follow that thread, and then come back and check its conclusions. So instead of just giving you a longer report, it could actually make progress on a research project—identify a promising direction, gather the evidence, and explain what’s still uncertain. But I’d want that extra time to translate into better work, not just more work. Can it recognize when it’s stuck? Can it change approaches? Can it verify what it’s found? That’s what would make a full day really valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says a full day could make progress on a research project, but it does not claim that it could complete research that would take a human weeks.
